Neonates of the Southern Ningaui (Ningaui yvonnae) enter the world at a wet weight at birth of just 0.005 grams [Wwb = 0.005 grams], a value typical of the extremely altricial newborns characteristic of dasyurid marsupials, where neonates are little more than embryos leaving the birth canal to complete development in the pouch. Under standard laboratory conditions mimicking the species' typical active-phase body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the gestation period is completed in a brief 17 days [tg = 17 days]. This compressed intrauterine phase, among the shortest recorded for any mammal of its body plan, reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid production of a litter over prolonged investment in a single embryo, a pattern that is ecologically advantageous in the unpredictable, resource-limited environments of the Australian arid zone where this species resides.

The pace of postnatal development in Ningaui yvonnae is tightly coupled to thermal conditions, with a sustained ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] being critical for the efficient metabolism of the altricial young. The time since birth at weaning, marking the transition to nutritional independence and the cessation of lactation, occurs at 78 days [tx = 78 days] under these optimal thermal conditions at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. At this critical juncture, a weaned juvenile, now capable of consuming solid invertebrate prey, typically achieves a wet weight of approximately 2.5 grams [Wwx = approximately 2.5 grams]. This value, which is based on allometric data from the congener Ningaui timealeyi, represents a substantial increase from the neonatal mass, yet it is still just a fraction of the adult size, indicating that a significant period of somatic growth and maturation lies ahead before the animal can enter the breeding population.

Sexual maturation in the Southern Ningaui is a protracted process relative to its rapid early development, reflecting the time required to build the necessary body size and physiological condition. The time since birth at puberty, a benchmark validated by studies on the closely related Ningaui timealeyi, is estimated at 290 days [tp = 290 days] when development proceeds at a consistent body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This extended juvenile phase, lasting nearly ten months, is likely an adaptation to the high energetic demands of reproduction in a small dasyurid. Upon reaching reproductive maturity, a clear sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size becomes apparent. Adult females attain an ultimate wet weight of 8.9 grams [Wwi = 8.9 grams], while males achieve a heavier ultimate wet weight of 10.4 grams [Wwi = 10.4 grams], a disparity likely linked to male-male competition for access to females during the brief, seasonal breeding window.

Reproductive output in Ningaui yvonnae under thermoneutral conditions maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C] is characterized by a low but consistent annual investment. Females are capable of producing a maximum of approximately 2 to 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 litters per year], with an average litter size of approximately 5.7 offspring per litter [N_R_i = approximately 5.7 offspring per litter]. This annual reproductive strategy translates to a moderate output, constrained by the short growing season and the energetic cost of supporting a litter of altricial young during the cool, dry winter months. The single annual breeding event, timed to coincide with the flush of insect prey following the Australian winter rains, maximizes the probability that the relatively small litter will survive through the weaning period. This life-history trade-off between fecundity and offspring investment is typical of small, insectivorous marsupials inhabiting seasonal environments.

The maximum lifespan for Ningaui yvonnae in a controlled laboratory setting, with a stable thermoneutral body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], has been recorded at approximately 20 months [am = approximately 20 months], a value that positions the Southern Ningaui as a relatively short-lived mammal, a characteristic common among small dasyurids that exhibit semelparous or near-semelparous reproductive strategies. The relatively brief lifespan is a direct consequence of a high metabolic rate and a life-history strategy that prioritizes a single, intensive breeding season over long-term survival. Males in particular often experience a sharp decline in condition and high mortality immediately following the mating period, a phenomenon attributed to the physiological stress of intense rutting behavior, which underscores the species' accelerated pace of life and rapid generational turnover in the wild.
